question: Where can a mathematical object stop behaving smoothly?
idea: A solution or shape may be well-behaved in some places and irregular in others. Understanding those irregularities helps distinguish a controlled solution from a possible breakdown. This entry studies the particular situation described below.
why: The study of smooth shapes, curvature, and how geometry changes from point to point.

glossary.meaning: A mathematical condition that rules out certain forms of escaping to infinity; in ordinary Euclidean space it means closed and bounded.
A shape is convex if the straight segment between any two of its points stays inside the shape.
A place where an object or solution fails to have the expected smooth or regular behavior.
A claim that, within specified conditions, there is only one possible solution or object.

exactClaim: Proves the first-singular-time case of tangent-flow uniqueness for smooth compact connected embedded surfaces without boundary in ℝ3. At every singular point, all fixed-center backward tangent flows agree as area measures at every negative time in the original ambient coordinates, without mean-convexity or a prescribed tangent model.
scope: A definition-led reading guide; the exact mathematical claim is preserved separately. This is not a proof assessment.
